question: You receive an unexpected message asking you to urgently verify your password. What should you do?

options.B: Reply with your password
options.C: Verify through an official trusted channel
options.D: Forward your credentials to your manager

explanation: Legitimate services never need your password by message. Urgency is a classic pressure tactic; verify via a channel you already trust and report the message.

question: An email's link text shows your bank's address, but hovering reveals a different domain. What does this indicate?

options.B: A likely phishing link - the real destination differs

explanation: A mismatch between displayed text and the real destination is a strong phishing indicator. Go to the bank by typing its address or using a bookmark.

question: A poster in the lobby has a QR code saying 'Scan to log in to the new staff portal'. What is the safest action?

options.B: Scan it but use a fake password
options.C: Check with IT through the official intranet before using it

explanation: QR codes hide the destination and can lead to credential-harvesting pages ('quishing'). Confirm through official channels first.

question: What is the MOST helpful thing to do after spotting a phishing email at work?

options.B: Report it using the official reporting button/channel
options.C: Reply to tell the sender you know it's fake
options.D: Forward it to all colleagues as a warning

explanation: Reporting lets the security team block the sender and find others who received it. Replying confirms your address is active; mass-forwarding spreads the lure.

question: Which password practice is the strongest?

options.B: A unique long passphrase for each account, stored in a password manager
options.C: Your pet's name plus the year

explanation: Uniqueness stops one breach from unlocking other accounts, and length makes guessing impractical. A password manager makes this realistic.

question: Why is password reuse dangerous?

options.A: It makes passwords harder to remember
options.B: Attackers try leaked passwords on many other sites (credential stuffing)
options.D: It is not dangerous if the password is long

explanation: Leaked credentials are automatically replayed against other services. Even a long password is unsafe once it has leaked.

question: Someone from 'IT support' asks for your password to fix your account. What should you do?

options.B: Give only half of it
options.C: Refuse and report the request; real IT staff never need your password
options.D: Email it instead of saying it

explanation: IT administrators can reset access without knowing your password. Requests for passwords are a social-engineering red flag.

question: Which is generally stronger?

options.B: Summer2026

explanation: A long passphrase of random words has far more possible combinations than short 'complex' passwords, and is easier to remember.

question: You get several MFA push notifications you did not request. What is the best response?

options.B: Deny them, change your password, and report it

explanation: Unrequested prompts usually mean someone already has your password and is trying 'MFA fatigue'. Deny, change the password and report.

question: Why is 'strong password + MFA' generally safer than a password alone?

options.B: An attacker also needs your second factor, not just the stolen password

explanation: MFA adds an independent factor, so stolen or guessed passwords alone are usually not enough to sign in.

question: Which MFA method is most resistant to phishing?

options.B: Email one-time code

explanation: Passkeys and FIDO2 keys are cryptographically bound to the real website, so they do not work on look-alike phishing sites and there is no code to steal.

question: A caller says they are from your bank and asks you to read out the code just sent to your phone. What should you do?

options.B: Hang up and call the bank using the number on its official website or card

explanation: One-time codes should never be shared. The caller is likely trying to complete a login or payment with your stolen details.

question: A 'senior executive' emails asking you to buy gift cards urgently and keep it confidential. What is this most likely?

options.B: A social-engineering / impersonation scam

explanation: Urgency, secrecy, authority and gift cards together are hallmark signs of executive impersonation fraud. Verify through a known channel.

question: A supplier emails new bank details for all future invoices. What should happen before paying?

options.B: Verify the change by calling the supplier on a number already on file
options.C: Reply to the email to confirm
options.D: Pay half to the old account and half to the new

explanation: Replying to the same email may reach the attacker. Call-back verification using known contact details defeats payment-redirection fraud.

question: Someone without a visible badge asks you to hold the secure door because their hands are full. What is the best action?

options.B: Politely direct them to reception or security to be let in
options.D: Ignore it and walk away without saying anything

explanation: 'Tailgating' exploits politeness. Directing visitors to reception keeps access control intact without being rude.

question: What makes social engineering effective?

options.A: It exploits human trust, fear, urgency and helpfulness
options.B: It needs advanced hacking skills
options.C: It only works on old computers

explanation: Social engineering targets human instincts rather than technology, and can happen by phone, chat, SMS, email or in person.

question: What does the padlock (HTTPS) icon in a browser guarantee?

options.A: The site is safe and legitimate
options.B: The connection is encrypted - not that the site is trustworthy
options.D: The site is run by a bank

explanation: Phishing sites commonly use HTTPS. The padlock only means traffic is encrypted between you and that site.

question: A pop-up says your computer is infected and to call a support number now. What should you do?

options.B: Install the software it recommends
options.C: Close the browser/tab and report it if unsure

explanation: Real security tools don't ask you to call numbers from web pop-ups. These are tech-support scams.

question: Where should you download software from?

options.A: Any site that ranks first in search results
options.B: Official vendor sites or approved app stores

explanation: Search ads and look-alike sites often distribute trojanised installers. Use official or organisation-approved sources.

question: Why should you remove browser extensions you don't use?

options.B: Extensions can read page data, and abandoned or sold extensions can become malicious

explanation: Extensions often have broad permissions. Reducing them reduces your attack surface.

question: Files on your computer suddenly have strange extensions and a ransom note appears. What is the FIRST thing to do?

options.B: Disconnect from the network and report to the security team immediately

explanation: Isolating the device limits spread; fast reporting lets responders act. Payment does not guarantee recovery and may fund further crime.

question: Which control most helps an organisation RECOVER from ransomware?

options.B: A bigger monitor

explanation: Backups that ransomware can't reach or alter allow restoration without paying, as long as restores are tested.

question: What is 'double extortion' in ransomware?

options.A: Asking for payment twice for the same key
options.B: Encrypting data AND threatening to leak stolen data

explanation: Many groups steal data before encrypting it, so backups alone don't remove the leak threat. Data protection and monitoring matter too.

question: Which is a common way ransomware gets into organisations?

options.A: Phishing emails and stolen remote-access passwords
options.B: Screen savers

explanation: Phishing, exposed remote access without MFA, and unpatched internet-facing systems are frequent entry points.

question: What does 'data minimisation' mean?

options.B: Collecting and keeping only the personal data you actually need

explanation: Less data collected means less data that can be lost, leaked or misused.

question: You accidentally emailed a spreadsheet of customer data to the wrong person. What should you do?

options.B: Report it immediately through the official process
options.C: Send a second email asking them to ignore it and tell nobody

explanation: Data protection laws often have strict notification deadlines. Early reporting lets the organisation contain the impact.

question: Is it safe to paste confidential customer records into a public, unapproved AI chatbot?

options.B: No - use only approved tools and follow data-handling policy
options.C: Yes, if you delete the chat after

explanation: Unapproved services may store or process data outside your organisation's control.

question: What is the safest sharing setting for a document containing personal data?

options.B: Public on the web
options.C: Specific named people who need access

explanation: Least privilege: share only with people who need access, and avoid open links for sensitive data.

question: You need to work from an airport with open public Wi-Fi. What is the safest option?

options.B: Use your organisation's VPN or your phone's hotspot

explanation: A VPN encrypts traffic over untrusted networks; a personal hotspot avoids the public network entirely.

question: You see two networks named 'CoffeeShop_WiFi' and 'CoffeeShop_WiFi_Free'. What could this be?

options.B: A possible 'evil twin' fake access point

explanation: Attackers can create look-alike hotspots to intercept traffic. Ask staff for the correct network name.

question: Which is the best home Wi-Fi security setting?

options.B: WEP
options.C: WPA3 (or WPA2-AES) with a strong passphrase

explanation: WPA3/WPA2-AES provide modern encryption. WEP is broken and hiding the SSID alone is not security.

question: What should you change on a new home router first?

options.B: The colour of the LEDs

explanation: Default admin credentials are widely known and a common way home routers are taken over.

question: An SMS says a parcel is held and asks you to pay a small fee via a link. What should you do?

options.A: Pay - it is only a small amount
options.B: Ignore the link and check delivery status in the official courier app or website

explanation: Delivery 'smishing' is common. Small fees are used to steal card details. Use official apps/sites instead of links.

question: A flashlight app requests access to your contacts, microphone and location. What should you do?

options.B: Deny unnecessary permissions or choose a different app

explanation: Permissions should match an app's purpose. Excessive permissions can indicate data harvesting.

question: What should you enable in case your phone is lost?

options.B: A louder ringtone only

explanation: Remote lock/wipe protects email, MFA apps and data on a lost device.

question: Where should you install apps from?

options.B: Official app stores (or your organisation's approved catalogue)
options.C: Any website offering a free version of a paid app

explanation: Sideloaded apps skip store security checks and are a common malware source.

question: You clicked a suspicious link and entered your password before realising. What is the best next step?

options.A: Say nothing and hope for the best
options.B: Change your password from a trusted device and report it immediately
options.C: Wait a week to see what happens

explanation: Fast reporting lets the security team revoke sessions and check activity. Reporting in good faith is always the right choice.

question: Which details are MOST useful in an incident report?

options.B: What happened, when, which device/account, and what you already did

explanation: Clear facts about time, systems and actions taken help responders triage and contain quickly.

question: You're not sure if an email is malicious. Should you report it?

options.B: Yes - reporting suspicious items is encouraged even if they turn out harmless
options.D: Only after clicking the link to check

explanation: Security teams would rather assess a harmless report than miss a real attack. Never click to 'test' it.

question: Why shouldn't you delete a suspicious email or file before reporting it?

options.B: It is evidence that helps responders investigate and protect others

explanation: Preserving evidence (headers, attachments, links) lets the security team block and search for related activity.
